name: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)
coverage: national (all US states, counties, and many cities/metro areas)
granularity: county and city, rolls up to metro area, state, census region/division
update_frequency: monthly, with an annual benchmark revision
history: decades of history available (varies by series, commonly back to the 1990s or earlier for most counties)

license.notes: US federal agency (Bureau of Labor Statistics) statistical product, public domain. The Public Data API v1 works with no registration; v2 (registration, still free) just raises the daily query cap and adds net/percent-change fields.

cost: free; v1 API unregistered cap is low (25 queries/day, max 10 years per query), registering for v2 (still free) raises it to 500 queries/day and a 20-year window
gap_addressed: The growth score's 'demographics' pillar (neighborhood.py) currently only has census_acs.py (income/population/education, refreshed twice a year off ACS 5-year estimates -- slow-moving). County-level monthly unemployment would be a faster-moving, independent economic-growth signal for the same pillar or a new one.

correlation.notes: evaluate_series.py doesn't exist yet. Worth flagging: BLS itself states county-level LAUS is not seasonally adjusted, so a naive month-over-month read is noisy and would need a trailing-12-month or year-over-year transform before it's a usable input -- more preprocessing than the other candidates need.

recommendation: Usable but the weakest of this batch on a value/effort basis. It's genuinely free and national, but NYC (5 counties, effectively one series each) gets little marginal signal from county-level unemployment versus the more granular ACS demographics already in place, the not-seasonally-adjusted data needs extra smoothing to be usable, and BLS series IDs have to be looked up per geography (more adapter complexity than a bulk CSV pull). Would matter more once the project has non-NYC neighborhoods with real county-level variation. Recommend holding this one rather than implementing now.
